source_text: {ΠΑΛΛ.} Διασάφει δὴ οὖν ὅ τί ποτ' ἐστὶν ὅ φησιν ὁ νόμος; {ΚΥΡ.} Ἀμυδρὸν, ὦ Παλλάδιε, τῆς ἐμπωλῆς τὸ χρῆμα, καὶ λίαν ἀνάντη τὴν προσβολὴν ἔχον, κἂν εἰ ἐν ψιλαῖς ἐννοίαις αὐτὴν περινοεῖν ἕλοιτό τις· φράσω γε μὴν, ὡς ἔνι, καὶ ὡς ἂν εἰς νοῦν ἴοι τὸν ἐμόν. Ἐρήσομαι δὲ, καί μοι λέγε· Τοῖς καταδῃοῦν εἰωθόσι πόλεις τε καὶ χώρας, τίνες ἂν εἶεν ἁλώσιμοι, καὶ οὐ σὺν ἱδρῶτι μακρῷ; πότερα δὴ φὴς, οἱ τειχῶν ἔσω καὶ πόλεων τῶν εὐπυργοτάτων, ἢ μᾶλλον οἱ ἐν ἀγροῖς; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Καὶ τίνι τοῦτο ἀσυμφανές; εὐαλωτότατοι γὰρ οἱ ἐν ἀτειχίστοι
pass_a_gloss: §14 dual gloss: εὐάλωτος / easily-caught · ἀτείχιστος / unwalled · ἀγροῖκος / rustic … Pass A scaffolding ≠ Pass B continuous English. Theme: Walled city = Jews; open fields = nations; who is easily taken.
pass_b_english: Palladius: So then clarify what ever it is the law says.

Cyril: Dim, O Palladius, is the matter of the sale, and having a very uphill approach, even if someone should choose to think it around in bare thoughts; yet I will speak, as possible, and as it would go into my mind. And I will ask, and tell me; For those accustomed to ravage cities and lands, who would be catchable, and not with long sweat? Which then do you say, those inside walls and of the most well-towered cities, or rather those in fields?
Palladius: And for whom is this unclear? for most easily-caught are those in unwalled fields.

Cyril: You spoke rightly; and whom do you think live through better and most fairly, city ones then and those in knowledge of laws, or those reared more rusticly in villages? So then more weakly will those in fields stand-before their own salvation, and those inside towered cities will counsel the better things, and will reckon lawfully the necessary things for themselves unto benefit, and when there is a time of counsel and plans.
Palladius: True; even if they have somehow suffered the being worsted.

Cyril: And indeed also for those in field, and having missed the best counsel, one might sometimes forgive the being caught; for unwalled and more uncounselled than those in the cities. Yet the others one might charge, and very reasonably I think, if after having warded off the enemies and saved the own things, by the assaults of those having stood opposite, they themselves willingly betrayed, and having been worsted beforehand by their own cowardice, have become under hand of those having stood opposite.

Cyril: So then see Jews, dwelling the holy city, about which the God of the wholes says: ‘And I will be for it, says Lord, a wall of fire in a circle, and unto glory I will be in midst of it.’ (Zechariah 2:5) And indeed also having been made wise toward this by law. Therefore also they were saying: ‘Blessed are we the sons of Israel, because the things pleasing to Lord are known for us.’ (Baruch 4:4) So then, do you not say such ones are altogether most hard-to-enter for the assaults of the demons, if at least they should choose to live rightly, and to be borne under the divine laws?

Cyril: And the herds of the nations, having the more rustic and easily-beside mind, would reasonably be altogether not with sweat takeable, for the plundering Satan, bare of the help from above, and least enriching the pedagogue law.
Cyril: So then Jews, those dwelling a city
